slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: BUN is often part of a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) and helps diagnose or monitor kidney diseases. Because early kidney disease usually has no signs or symptoms, it is also used to screen people at risk.
BUN is often interpreted together with blood creatinine from the same panel (one of the test’s other names is BUN-to-creatinine ratio); this comparison can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: MedlinePlus covers this analyte as the BUN (blood urea nitrogen) test, which measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood. Urea nitrogen is a waste product formed as the body breaks down proteins; it is carried in blood and removed by the kidneys in urine.

slides.title: Urea
cols: A high BUN generally suggests that the kidneys are not working well. Other possible causes include dehydration, burns, certain medicines, a high-protein diet and a recent heart attack.
Possible causes of a low BUN include a lack of protein in the diet, malnutrition and liver disease.

slides.title: Urea
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting for several hours may be required.
Limitations: BUN levels vary with sex and usually increase with age. An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
BUN is only one measure of kidney function. If kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed, such as creatinine and GFR, which estimates how well the kidneys filter blood.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: G1 ≥90; G2 60–89; G3a 45–59; G3b 30–44; G4 15–29; G5 <15 (if persisting >3 months) mL/min/1.73 m²

slides.title: What does the BUN test actually measure?
options: Total protein in the blood, from which urea nitrogen is formed
Creatinine, a waste product released from muscle and removed by the kidneys
Urea nitrogen, a waste product of protein breakdown removed by the kidneys
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: BUN measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the BUN test measures urea nitrogen in blood; urea nitrogen forms when proteins are broken down and is removed by the kidneys.

slides.title: A person who has been drinking very little fluid has a high BUN. Which statement matches the source?
options: A high BUN always means kidney disease, whatever the person’s fluid intake has been.
Dehydration is one possible cause of a high BUN, and an abnormal result does not always mean a condition needing treatment.
Dehydration typically lowers BUN rather than raising it, so this high result must reflect a kidney disease needing treatment.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: dehydration is listed among causes of high BUN; if kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed.

Basis: MedlinePlus: dehydration is a possible cause of high BUN; abnormal results don’t always mean a condition needing treatment.

Residual nitrogen. Azotemias. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. "Residual nitrogen" is the nitrogen in the protein-free filtrate (urea ~50%, amino acids, uric acid, creatinine, ammonia, etc.); this summary parameter is historical, individual components are measured now.

2. Azotemia is an increase of nitrogenous substances (urea, creatinine) in the blood: prerenal (reduced renal perfusion – dehydration, heart failure, hemorrhage; the urea/creatinine ratio is usually >20:1 (in mg/dL)), renal (parenchymal damage), postrenal (urinary tract obstruction).
3. Productional (extrarenal) increase of urea: high protein intake, catabolism, GI bleeding, glucocorticoids.

slides.title: Residual nitrogen. Azotemias. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 4. Assessing kidney function: creatinine (the enzymatic method is preferred) and eGFR, cystatin C if needed; urea and uric acid are auxiliary.
5. Decrease of urea: severe liver failure, protein deficiency, pregnancy, fluid overload.

slides.title: Methods of determining urea?
bullets: 1. The main method is enzymatic: urease cleaves urea into ammonia and CO2, and ammonia consumes NADH in the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction – the decrease in absorbance at 340 nm is measured kinetically.
2. Other variants: urease + conductometry or an ion-selective electrode; non-automated colorimetric methods (for example diacetyl monoxime) – historical.
3. Sample: serum/plasma (ammonium heparin is not used – ammonia contamination), urine.
4. Expressing the result: urea (mmol/L) or blood urea nitrogen (BUN, mg/dL); know the conversion.

slides.title: Methods of determining urea?
bullets: 5. Clinical significance: types of azotemia, urea/creatinine ratio (high in the prerenal state), dialysis adequacy; urea depends more on diet and catabolism than GFR does.

slides.title: Methods of determining urea in blood and clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. Methods: urease–glutamate dehydrogenase kinetic UV method (decrease of NADH at 340 nm) – the main one on automated analyzers; urease + conductometry/ion-selective electrode; urease Berthelot colorimetric method.
2. Sample: serum or plasma (not ammonium anticoagulant); avoid hemolysis and ammonia contamination.
3. Increase (azotemia): prerenal (dehydration, heart failure, shock, GI bleeding), renal (acute/chronic kidney disease), postrenal (obstruction); catabolism, protein-rich food, glucocorticoids.

slides.title: Methods of determining urea in blood and clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 4. Decrease: severe liver failure (urea synthesis falls), protein deficiency, pregnancy, overhydration.
5. Interpretation together with creatinine/eGFR; the urea/creatinine ratio helps to suggest a prerenal state, but its diagnostic value is limited.
